A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Sparse ActionGen. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and can be matched despite reformatting, relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: V1 reports original simulation benchmarks, component ablations, pruning analyses and a physical pick-and-release experiment.

after.justification: V2 retains original simulation results and reports additional physical-robot, sampler, pruning-budget and observation-robustness experiments.

M1.justification: The observation-conditioned pruner, architecture, fidelity and sparsity losses, shared caches and training/inference procedures remain unchanged. Equations 1–13 and Algorithms 1–2 retain their substance. The DPM-Solver++ experiment tests compatibility without introducing a new SAG component.

E1.justification: V1's physical pick-and-release task is replaced by Stack Bowls, Insert Pen and Assembly Line in v2. Appendix A.11 adds simulation scenarios involving lighting, background tint, distractors and occlusion, plus physical hand-occlusion, laser-distraction and low-light scenarios. The original RoboMimic and Kitchen coverage remains.

E2.justification: V2 Table 5 adds DPM-Solver++ comparisons, evaluating DPM10 and DPM50 against DPM50+SAG. Existing simulation comparators and the comparator set in Figure 5 remain. 'Full Precision' becoming 'Full Computation' is a rename; additional CP step budgets change settings rather than comparator identity.

E3.justification: New protocols include 10/50-step DPM-Solver++ comparisons, success-rate evaluation at 80%, 91% and 97% pruning, and approximately compute-matched CP/SAG comparisons at effective budgets of 3, 9 and 20 steps. V2 also introduces controlled visual perturbations. Its replacement physical tasks use 200 demonstrations each, versus 150 for v1's former task. Retained simulation benchmark settings are unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component ablations and training curves, v2 adds sampler compatibility, pruning-rate sensitivity, compute-matched comparisons, aggregate block-participation analysis and simulation/physical observation-robustness tests. These examine complementary acceleration, budget fairness, computation allocation and failure conditions absent from v1's analyses.

E5.justification: V2 Table 11 explicitly reports successes over 20 trials for each physical robustness condition, adding trial-repetition information. The three fixed simulation seeds and uncertainty entries in retained Tables 1–3 are unchanged. No increased repetition of retained experiments, new confidence intervals or significance tests is established.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3, existing latency values and per-task component-ablation results are retained, but substantial new results appear. V1 Figure 5's pick-and-release result of 54% success at 40.5 Hz is replaced by results on different physical tasks, including Assembly Line at 58% and 44.3 Hz; these are not same-setting improvements. New findings include average success of 85% at 91% pruning versus 51% at 97%, sampler/budget comparisons and zero successes under low light. The specific pruner-overhead figure of less than 0.3% FLOPs is removed.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation, objectives and cache-update equations remain substantively identical. Neither version supplies formal theorems or proofs, and v2's additional experimental budget comparisons do not introduce a new theoretical result.

C1.justification: The introduction and contribution list narrow 'lossless' or no-sacrifice acceleration to maintaining comparable task performance. The central contributions, greater-than-90% pruning and up-to-4× acceleration claims remain. This qualification is incomplete because the abstract still says 'without sacrificing performance'.

C2.justification: V2 interprets extreme-pruning failures as losing computations needed for fine corrections, explains sampler complementarity, and attributes severe observation-shift failures primarily to the underlying policy. Its new Limitations section identifies dependence on fixed budgets, representative training data and the evaluated policy/platform scope. These substantially expand applicability and mechanism discussion. The new Impact Statement nevertheless contradicts the physical experiments by describing all experiments as simulation.

D1.justification: V2 documents a front-view camera and 200 demonstrations per new physical task, and specifies the 100-step DDPM schedule used in its budget comparison. Most hardware, optimizer, training-split and hyperparameter information is relocated unchanged to Appendix A.3. Project and pretrained-checkpoint access information is retained.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations to DiTA and Test-time Sparsity for Extreme Fast Action Diffusion, while removing VGGT-DP and TS-DP. The broader positioning against static caching, block-wise reuse and distillation remains substantially unchanged; moving Related Work earlier does not itself change that positioning.

P1.justification: Most existing prose is retained. Related Work moves before Methodology, implementation details move into the appendix, and wording around caching, evaluation and the conclusion is refined. Author metadata and baseline terminology change, the LLM-use disclosure is removed, and new analysis, limitations and acknowledgment/impact sections are inserted.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column main-text layout and extensively resizes and relocates displays. It merges the two ablation-table panels, replaces Figure 5's physical-task display, revises diagram labels and captions, and adds six tables plus block-participation Figures 14–15. Existing appendix plots are retained and rearranged.

improvement.justification: V1 leaves pruning tolerance, compute-matched competitiveness and observation-shift behavior largely untested. V2 directly investigates these issues through its sensitivity study and Appendices A.5 and A.11, while broadening physical validation and explicitly documenting failure conditions. This substantially strengthens the evidence and clarifies applicability. Limited uncertainty reporting, the incompletely qualified abstract and the contradictory simulation-only Impact Statement temper the improvement but do not outweigh these gains.
